Optima Academy Online · Discovering Computer Science

A Letter of Welcome 🦉

To our explorer-scholars and the families who travel with them.

Dear Students and Families,

Welcome to Discovering Computer Science. I'm [Instructor name], and I'll be your guide this year as we take on a single, surprisingly large question: what is computer science, and why is it worth learning even if you never write code for a living?

Our answer is that computing is a liberal art — a lens for interpreting the world, as worth studying as literature or logic. So we'll treat this year as an expedition. Each unit charts a new territory on the map of computing: the machine, the network, the logic of programs, algorithms and data, the command line, the programmer's craft, security, and finally intelligence and citizenship in a digital age. In every territory we do three things — build something with our hands, read a foundational text by the people who invented the field (Lovelace, Turing, Berners-Lee, and others), and argue about what it means.

What to expect

  • Self-paced, mastery-based. There's a suggested weekly pace, but students move forward when they've shown they understand — not when the clock says so. Checkpoints can be retaken; they exist for learning, not for gotchas.
  • Online, and social anyway. No live attendance is required, but this is not a solo course. Students post and respond in our discussion board, give real feedback on each other's work, and keep a logbook of reflections. Their writing is their presence here, and it counts toward their grade.
  • Real tools, no special equipment. A computer and a modern web browser are all that's needed. Programming happens in free, browser-based environments; circuits and devices are explored through simulators. A VR headset is optional enrichment — never required, and nothing is hidden behind it.
  • Honest work, including with AI. AI tools may be used to explain, unstick, and check reasoning — then students write and code it themselves, disclose the help, and stand ready to explain their work. We treat this as a skill to learn, not a temptation to police.

How families can help

  • Help your student protect a steady weekly rhythm. Self-paced courses reward routine and punish drift more than any other kind.
  • Ask them what they're building, and ask them to explain it to you. Explaining is the fastest way to find out what you actually understand.
  • Let the struggle happen. A stuck program is not a failure — it's the assignment. Encourage them to post the question rather than abandon the problem.
Access and accommodations. Every activity is self-paced with no time limit, readings are provided as text, and videos are captioned. If your student has an IEP or 504 plan, or needs an alternative format, message me at the start of the course — supports are arranged confidentially.

Reaching me

Message me anytime in Canvas or email [instructor email]; I reply [response time]. There are optional office hours each quarter, and questions are always welcome in the discussion board — often another student has the same one.

One last thing about how I teach. I'm a lead learner, not an oracle. Computing changes faster than any of us can keep up with, and I will happily say "I don't know" in front of a class — right before we go find out. That posture is the course.

I'm glad you're here. Let's go draw the map.

Warmly,
[Instructor name]
Discovering Computer Science · Optima Academy Online

pages.title: Course Syllabus
pages.html:
Optima Academy Online · Florida Course #0200384

Discovering Computer Science

🦉 An expedition into the liberal art of computing.
Course Discovering Computer Science (#0200384) · Year-long elective · Grades 9–12 · Level 2
Format Fully online · self-paced / asynchronous · VR-capable (VR optional, never required)
Instructor [Instructor name] · [instructor email]
Async help Message me in Canvas; I respond [response time]. Optional office hours & live VR experiences each quarter.

Course Description

Discovering Computer Science introduces you to the fundamental principles of computer science, emphasizing its role as a tool for problem-solving, communication, and personal expression. We explore the visible, impactful aspects of computing — how it shapes the world around us — through the design process, data that solves real problems, and the input/output of physical computing (here, via simulators). Through hands-on projects and real-world applications you build the skills to interpret and influence the digital world, whether or not you pursue a career in technology.

Computer science as a liberal art. Computing is fundamental to understanding and participating in modern society, so it is worth learning as part of a liberal education — a critical lens for interpreting the world. In this course we travel that idea as an expedition: each unit is a new territory on the map of computing, charted through a foundational reading, a hands-on activity, and shared inquiry. You are an explorer-scholar, and I am your lead learner — my mantra is, "I may not know every answer, but together we can figure it out."

How This Self-Paced Course Works

  • Suggested pace: a recommended weekly plan keeps you on track to finish in the school year, but you advance when you have demonstrated mastery — not by the clock.
  • Waypoints (mastery checkpoints): short auto-graded checks gate each leg of the journey. Retake them until you reach mastery; they are for learning, not gotchas.
  • Learning is social — asynchronously. You will post and respond in the Agora (discussion boards), give and receive structured feedback in the Council (peer review), keep a Logbook of written/recorded reflections, and publish shared artifacts. No live attendance is required.
  • Getting help: message me anytime in Canvas (I reply [response time]); post questions in the Agora; join optional quarterly office hours or live VR experiences.

The Expedition: Units & Primary Sources

Unit (Territory) Strand focus Primary-source anchor
0 · Base Camp — the Computational CommonsCommunication & collaboration; integrity & responsible AIWing, "Computational Thinking" (2006)
1 · The Machine — hardware & originsComputing systems; I/O (simulators)Moore, "Cramming More Components" (1965)
2 · The Network — connection & the InternetNetworks; the InternetBerners-Lee, "Information Management" (1989)
3 · The Logic of Programs — the explorer's languageProgramming foundations (Code.org / p5.js)Lovelace, Note G (1843)
4 · Algorithms, Data & IntelligenceAlgorithms; data; modeling; intro MLDijkstra, "Go To Considered Harmful" (1968)
5 · Command of the Machine — the command-line frontierProgramming (shell); systems in practiceKernighan & Pike, Unix Programming Environment
6 · The Programmer's Craft — scripting & building togetherScripting; software engineering; collaboration; licensesACM Code of Ethics + open-source licenses
7 · Guarding the Republic — security & cryptographyCybersecurity; cryptography; online safetyKerckhoffs' principle + breach case study
8 · Intelligence & the Digital Citizen — draw your own map (capstone)AI & emerging tech; society, ethics & well-beingTuring, "Computing Machinery & Intelligence" (1950)

Suggested pacing: Units 0–4 in Semester 1; Units 5–8 in Semester 2. Programming runs all year — visual & creative coding (Code.org App Lab, p5.js) in Semester 1, then the command-line and scripting arc as core work in Semester 2.

Standards Alignment

This course is built to Florida's B.E.S.T. Standards for Computer Science (effective July 2024) for course #0200384, and intentionally embeds Florida's Computational Thinking & Reasoning (CTR), Mathematical Thinking & Reasoning (MTR), ELA Expectations (EE), and English Language Development (ELD) standards.

The seven CS strands (SC.912.*) covered:

  • CC — Communication & Collaboration
  • CO — Computing Systems / Organization
  • CS — Cybersecurity
  • ET — Emerging Technologies
  • HS — Health, Safety & Digital Citizenship
  • PE — Programming
  • TI — Technology & Information (impact, ethics, law)

Embedded throughout: SC.K12.CTR.*, MA.K12.MTR.*, ELA.K12.EE.*, and ELD.K12.ELL.SI.1.

Materials & Technology

  • Canvas — your home base for all lessons, discussions, and assessments.
  • Code.org CS Discoveries (App Lab / Game Lab) and the p5.js web editor / Trinket — programming environments.
  • MakeCode micro:bit and Tinkercad Circuits simulators — physical-computing concepts (input/output, circuits). No hardware required; simulators cover the I/O concepts in the standards.
  • Interactive activities hosted by the course on the web and embedded in Canvas (concept explorations, algorithm visualizations, a safe command-line sandbox, cipher tools).
  • A modern web browser (Chrome/Edge/Firefox/Safari). A VR headset is optional for enrichment experiences only.

Grading & Progress

Progress, not seat-time. Your grade reflects what you produce and how you contribute — milestones reached, artifacts created, and the quality of your participation in the Agora and the Council — not hours logged.

CategoryWeight*What it includes
Projects & Waypoint artifacts40%Rubric-graded unit projects + the capstone ("Draw Your Own Map").
Discussions & peer review (Agora & Council)25%Required. Post-and-respond threads + structured async peer review (you are graded on the feedback you give, too).
Mastery checks (Waypoints)20%Auto-graded formative quizzes; retakes encouraged until mastery.
Logbook reflections15%Written or recorded reflections connecting readings, code, and ideas.

*Provisional weights — confirm against OAO grading policy before publishing.

Academic Integrity & Responsible Use of AI

Your work must be your own. Plagiarism, misrepresenting others' digital work as yours, falsifying data, and uncited copying are violations of academic integrity.

Using AI responsibly. AI tools (chatbots, code assistants) can support your learning — like a tutor or a reference — but they do not replace your thinking, and they are not always right. In this course:

  • Use AI to explain concepts, get unstuck, or check your reasoning — then write/code it yourself and be ready to explain it.
  • Disclose when and how you used an AI tool on a graded artifact (a one-line note is fine).
  • Never submit AI output as your own original work, and never paste confidential or personal data into AI tools.
  • On peer review and collaborative projects, irresponsible AI use (e.g., fabricated feedback or data) undermines your teammates and violates TI.2.6.

This section will be reconciled with Optima Classical Academy's official academic-integrity and AI-use policy language before publishing.

Accommodations

Optima Academy Online provides accommodations for students with disabilities as identified in an Individual Educational Plan (IEP) or Section 504 plan, consistent with federal and Florida law. Accommodations may include adjusted time demands and schedules, alternative instructional materials and formats, assistive technology, and modified assignments or assessments. Please share your plan with me at the start of the course so supports can be arranged; documentation is kept confidential. This course is built to WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility standards, and its self-paced design supports extended time by default.

Our Asynchronous Community Norms

  • Be present in writing. Since we rarely meet live, your posts and feedback are your presence here. Contribute generously.
  • Cite your evidence and use a respectful, scholarly voice in the Agora and the Council.
  • Treat errors as discoveries. Bugs and wrong turns are how explorers learn — share them.
  • Respond, don't just post. Read peers' work, build on their ideas, and disagree kindly with reasons.
  • Reach out early. If you're stuck or falling behind the suggested pace, message me — that's what a lead learner is for.

pages.title: 0.01 What Is Computer Science? (CS as a Liberal Art)
pages.html:
Unit 0 · Lesson 0.01

What Is Computer Science? (And Why Call It a Liberal Art?)

I can…
  • define computational thinking and give an example in my own life;
  • explain what it means to call computer science a "liberal art" — a way of seeing the world;
  • cite evidence from a text to support a claim.

🧭 The hook

You already think computationally — you just may not call it that. When you plan the fastest route between three errands, sort laundry into loads, or follow a recipe, you are decomposing problems, spotting patterns, and following algorithms. In 2006 a computer scientist named Jeannette Wing argued that this kind of thinking belongs next to reading, writing, and arithmetic as a skill everyone should learn. Let's read her case.

📜 Primary source

Jeannette M. Wing, "Computational Thinking." Communications of the ACM, Vol. 49, No. 3 (March 2006), pp. 33–35. A 3-page essay — short, but dense. Read it twice.

📄 Read the essay (PDF, Carnegie Mellon University) →

Access: the PDF includes selectable text for screen readers and text-to-speech. Prefer to listen? Use your browser's "Read aloud" / Immersive Reader. A short glossary is below.

Context: who, when, why it matters

Wing was head of computer science at Carnegie Mellon and later a leader at the U.S. National Science Foundation. This three-page essay is one of the most-cited pieces in computing education — it launched the phrase "computational thinking" into classrooms worldwide. She is not saying everyone should become a programmer; she's saying everyone benefits from the mental tools computer scientists use.

Read with these questions (you'll use them in the Agora)

  1. Wing writes that computational thinking is "a fundamental skill for everyone." What evidence or examples does she give to support that claim? (Cite a specific line.)
  2. She repeatedly contrasts what humans do well with what computers do well. Find one example of each.
  3. Wing calls abstraction the most important mental tool in computing. In your own words, what is abstraction, and why might it matter outside of computers?
  4. Where do you disagree with her, or want to push back? (It's okay — scholars argue.)
Glossary. Computational thinking — solving problems using ideas from computer science (decomposition, patterns, abstraction, algorithms). Abstraction — focusing on the important details and hiding the rest. Algorithm — a precise, ordered set of steps. Heuristic — a rule of thumb that usually works. Liberal art — a field studied to develop general understanding and reasoning, not only job skills.

🛠️ Explore: the Computational Thinking Toolkit

Wing's four big practices are easier to spot once you've named them. Try this short interactive: read each everyday scenario and choose the practice at work. It's keyboard-friendly and you can retry as many times as you like.

If the activity doesn't load inside Canvas, open it in a new tab: Computational Thinking Toolkit ↗

🏛️ Discuss in the Agora

Head to the discussion "Base Camp: Introductions & Is CS a Liberal Art?" Post your response (≈150–200 words), then reply to at least two classmates. Use evidence from Wing — quote a line and cite it.

Prompt: Introduce yourself in two sentences (what brought you here, and one thing you're curious about). Then: Do you find Wing's argument that computer science is "a fundamental skill for everyone" convincing? Quote one line as evidence, and give one example from your own life where computational thinking would help.

📖 Logbook (quick reflection)

In a sentence or two (typed or recorded): Before today, what did you think "computer science" meant? Did Wing change your mind? Keep this — you'll revisit it at the end of the year.

Accommodations & access. No time limit. Read or listen to the essay; respond in the Agora by typing or recording audio/video. Need a shorter annotated excerpt or another format? Message your instructor — provided confidentially per your IEP/504 plan.

pages.title: 0.03 Academic Integrity & Responsible AI Use
pages.html:
Unit 0 · Lesson 0.03

Academic Integrity & the Responsible Use of AI

I can…
  • explain what counts as academic dishonesty — including misrepresenting digital work;
  • use AI tools responsibly as a support for my learning, and disclose when I do;
  • give proper credit using citation tools.

The simple rule

Your work must be your own, and you give credit for everything that isn't. The following violate academic integrity — and the very standards we study in this course:

  • Plagiarism — using someone's words, code, images, or ideas without credit.
  • Misrepresenting digital work as your own — submitting another person's (or an AI's) output as if you created it.
  • Falsifying data — inventing or altering results.
  • Uncited copying — even with small edits.

🤖 Using AI like a scholar, not a shortcut

AI tools (chatbots, code assistants) can genuinely help you learn — like a tutor or a reference book. But they don't replace your thinking, and they are often confidently wrong. Part of being a responsible scholar is weighing how irresponsible information use — including AI — affects you and the people you collaborate with. Here's our policy:

✅ Responsible🚫 Not allowed
Ask AI to explain a concept, then write/code it yourself.Paste AI output and submit it as your own.
Use AI to get unstuck on a bug, then explain your fix.Have AI do an assignment you're meant to do yourself.
Disclose when/how you used a tool (a one-line note).Hide that you used AI.
Check AI claims against a trusted source.Submit fabricated facts, citations, or data from AI.
Keep your work and others' private.Paste personal or confidential data into AI tools.

Disclosure looks like: "I used an AI chatbot to explain recursion and to suggest test cases; I wrote all the code and the explanation myself."

Giving credit: citation tools

When you use a source — an article, a tutorial, an image, an AI tool — cite it. You don't have to memorize a format; use a citation tool (your library's generator, Canvas's, or a reputable online one) and be consistent. When in doubt, name the source and link it.

✍️ Do this: sign the Expedition Agreement

Open "Integrity & Responsible-AI Acknowledgement" and complete it. You'll answer two short scenarios and confirm you understand the policy. This is your ticket out of Base Camp.

Note for the instructor (remove before publishing): reconcile this page and the acknowledgement with Optima Classical Academy's official academic-integrity and AI-use policy language, and link the official handbook.
Accommodations & access. No time limit; respond by typing or recording. Need the policy read aloud or in another format? Message your instructor (confidential, per IEP/504).

Unit 1 · Territory One

The Machine: Hardware & Its Origins 🖥️

Our first territory is the machine itself. What is a computer made of, how do its parts work together, and how did it shrink from a room-sized giant to the device in your pocket? Time to open the case.

Your route through this territory

  1. 1.01 — Anatomy of a Machine
    The principal components — CPU, memory, storage, power, and the motherboard that ties them together.
  2. 1.02 — Input, Output & Files
    How data gets in and out (with circuit & micro:bit simulators), and how we choose file formats.
  3. 1.03 — The Operating System & Choosing Software
    What an OS does, how it differs from apps, and how to pick the right software for a job.
  4. 1.04 — The Machine Through Time
    Read Gordon Moore's famous 1965 prediction, explore a timeline of computing, and look at where the careers are.
  5. Waypoint 1
    A retakeable check on the parts of the machine and how computing has changed.

What you'll be able to do

  • Name a computer's principal components and describe what each one does.
  • Explain the difference between input and output, and between an operating system and an application.
  • Choose a file format — and a piece of software — by weighing real trade-offs.
  • Describe how hardware has changed over time, and make an evidence-based prediction about where it's headed.

The big project

This unit ends with "Spec Your Own Machine" — you'll design a computer build for a real person's needs and budget, justify every component choice, and forecast where technology in your build is heading. You'll pull together everything in this territory.

pages.title: 1.01 Anatomy of a Machine
pages.html:
Unit 1 · Lesson 1.01

Anatomy of a Machine

I can…
  • name a computer's principal components and say what each one does;
  • describe the CPU — cores, clock speed, and why they matter;
  • explain what a power supply unit does and why its wattage matters.

🧭 The hook

If you opened a laptop and a game console and a phone, you'd find the same kinds of parts inside, doing the same jobs. A computer isn't magic — it's an organized team of components, each with one role, connected so they can pass work back and forth. Learn the team, and every device makes more sense.

🛠️ Explore: open the case

Use the Computer Anatomy Explorer below. Select each component to learn its job, then take the quick match-up check at the bottom. Pay special attention to the CPU (the brain) and the power supply (the heart) — they come back on Waypoint 1.

Activity not loading in Canvas? Open it in a new tab: Computer Anatomy Explorer ↗

Key ideas to hold onto

ComponentIts one job
CPURuns instructions. More cores = more work at once; higher clock speed = faster per core; socket must match the motherboard.
RAMFast temporary memory for what's open now. Volatile — cleared at power-off.
StorageKeeps files permanently. SSD ≫ HDD for speed.
PSUConverts wall power to steady DC. Needs enough wattage; connector type and modularity matter.
MotherboardConnects everything so parts can communicate.

📖 Logbook (quick reflection)

In a sentence or two: which component surprised you most, and why? If you had to spend extra money on one part to make a computer feel faster, which would you pick — and what's your reasoning?

Accommodations & access. The explorer is fully keyboard-operable and screen-reader labeled; the component table repeats every fact in text. Respond to the Logbook by typing or recording. Need another format? Message your instructor (confidential, per IEP/504).

pages.title: 1.02 Input, Output & Files
pages.html:
Unit 1 · Lesson 1.02

Input, Output & Files

I can…
  • tell the difference between input and output, and give real examples of each;
  • trace how a signal becomes input, gets processed, and returns as output;
  • choose a file format by weighing size, quality, and accessibility.

🧭 Input in, output out

Every computer does the same loop: it takes in input (data from the world — a key press, a tap, a sensor reading), processes it, and sends back output (something you can see, hear, or feel — pixels, sound, a blinking light). A keyboard is input; a screen is output. A touchscreen is both. Learn to spot the loop and you can reason about any device.

🛠️ Explore: physical computing (in a simulator)

Honest note: we use simulators, not physical kits. A simulator fully covers the input/output concepts in this course — buttons, sensors, and displays behave just like the real thing on screen. If your class later gets a physical micro:bit or Arduino, the same code runs on the real board with no changes. No hardware is required to master this unit.

The BBC micro:bit is a tiny computer with buttons and a motion sensor for input and an LED grid for output. In the MakeCode editor below, build a small program: when button A is pressed (input), show a heart on the LEDs (output); when the board is shaken, show a different image. Press ▶ in the simulator to test it — no download needed.

If the editor doesn't load inside Canvas, open it in a new tab: MakeCode micro:bit ↗. You'll submit a snapshot of your working program in the "Signals In, Signals Out" activity.

Want to see input/output as an electrical circuit? Explore Tinkercad Circuits ↗ and wire a button (input) to an LED (output) on a virtual breadboard. (Tinkercad asks for a free login, so it opens in a new tab.)

Files: same idea, different trade-offs

When output is saved, it becomes a file — and the format you choose is a trade-off between size, quality, and accessibility (can others open it?). There's rarely one "right" format; there's the right format for the job.

JobA good pickWhy (trade-off)
Photo for the webJPGSmall file; some quality loss is invisible for photos.
Logo with sharp edges / transparencyPNG or SVGKeeps crisp edges; SVG scales to any size.
A document anyone can openPDFHighly accessible; looks the same everywhere.
Data for a spreadsheet/programCSVTiny, universal, easy for programs to read.

🏛️ Discuss in the Agora (optional short thread)

Post one everyday device and break it down: what's its input, what's its output, and what do you think it's doing in between? Reply to one classmate with a device that has a surprising input or output.

Accommodations & access. Simulators are pointer- and keyboard-operable and need no hardware. The MakeCode blocks also have a text-code view. Tables restate every idea in text. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

pages.title: 1.03 The Operating System & Choosing Software
pages.html:
Unit 1 · Lesson 1.03

The Operating System & Choosing Software

I can…
  • explain what an operating system does and how it differs from an application;
  • describe how a driver lets the OS talk to hardware;
  • judge how efficient and effective a digital tool is for a real task, and set criteria for choosing software.

🧭 The layer you never see

You click an app; it just works. Behind that click is the operating system (OS) — Windows, macOS, ChromeOS, Linux, Android, iOS — the master program that manages the hardware, memory, files, and every app running on top. Apps ask the OS for what they need; the OS decides how to give it to them.

OS vs. application — who does what?

Operating systemApplication
Manages hardware, memory, storage, and security for the whole machine.Does one job for you — a browser, a game, a word processor.
Always running while the computer is on.Runs only when you open it; asks the OS for resources.
One per device (usually).Many can run at once.

Drivers: the OS's translators

How does the OS talk to a specific printer, graphics card, or game controller when there are thousands of models? Through a driver — a small piece of software that acts as a communication bridge between one piece of hardware and the operating system. The OS speaks a general language; the driver translates it into exactly what that device understands. Plug in a new device and the OS often fetches its driver automatically.

The chain: Application → asks the → Operating System → uses a → Driver → to control the → Hardware.

Choosing software like a pro

When you (or a school, or a company) pick software for a task, you're really evaluating trade-offs. Good decision-makers set criteria first, then judge each option against them. Four that matter almost every time:

  • Cost — free, one-time, or subscription? What's the total over a year?
  • Features — does it actually do the job (and not much you'll never use)?
  • Reliability — is it stable, secure, and well-supported?
  • Usability — can the intended person actually use it without a struggle?

The "best" tool is the one that best fits the task and the user — a powerful tool that nobody can use efficiently is a poor choice. That's what it means to weigh a tool's efficiency and effectiveness for a real-world task.

pages.title: 1.04 The Machine Through Time
pages.html:
Unit 1 · Lesson 1.04

The Machine Through Time

I can…
  • describe how computer hardware has changed — smaller, faster, cheaper — over time;
  • read a primary source and cite evidence for a claim about technology trends;
  • connect these trends to real career paths in computing.

🧭 A room, then a pocket

The 1940s ENIAC weighed about 30 tons and filled a room. The phone in your pocket is millions of times more powerful. That's not an accident — it's a trend, and in 1965 an engineer named Gordon Moore put a number on it.

🛠️ Explore: the timeline

Walk the timeline below. Notice the pattern at each step: components get smaller, faster, and cheaper. The gold marker is Moore's Law — the trend we're about to read in the original.

Open in a new tab if needed: Computing Through the Ages ↗

📜 Primary source: Gordon Moore (1965)

Gordon E. Moore, "Cramming More Components onto Integrated Circuits." Electronics, Vol. 38, No. 8 (April 19, 1965). Short and historic — this is where "Moore's Law" begins.

📄 Read the original paper (PDF) →

Access note: the scanned PDF is images of the 1965 magazine, so screen readers can't read it aloud. Use the accessible excerpt below (and its plain-language summary) to do the reading and the discussion — you won't miss anything required.

Accessible excerpt (Moore's key claims, quoted)

"The complexity for minimum component costs has increased at a rate of roughly a factor of two per year… Certainly over the short term this rate can be expected to continue, if not to increase."

"Integrated circuits will lead to such wonders as home computers — or at least terminals connected to a central computer — automatic controls for automobiles, and personal portable communications equipment."

In plain language: Moore noticed that the number of components (transistors) manufacturers could fit on a chip — for the lowest cost — kept doubling in a regular way, and he bet it would keep going. He even predicted home computers and portable communicators. He was right for about 50 years. Notice: this was a prediction about a trend, not a law of nature.

Read with these questions (for the Agora)

  1. What exactly did Moore claim was doubling — and how often? (Quote the excerpt.)
  2. Which of Moore's 1965 predictions came true? Point to something in your own life as evidence.
  3. A trend is not a guarantee. What might cause Moore's Law to slow down or stop — and what have engineers done as it slows?

Where the trends lead: careers

Every shift in this timeline opened new kinds of work. Because computing keeps changing, technology careers keep multiplying — and many aren't what you'd expect:

  • Building it: software developer, hardware/chip engineer, network engineer.
  • Protecting it: cybersecurity analyst, privacy specialist.
  • Applying it: health-information tech, data analyst, UX designer, AI/ML specialist, IT support.
  • Computing + another field: nearly every industry — medicine, art, agriculture, law — now needs people who understand computing.

You'll research one of these paths in the unit project and make a short evidence-based forecast about where it's heading.

🏛️ Discuss in the Agora

Go to "Moore's Law: Trend or Destiny?" Post your take (≈150 words) using evidence from Moore's excerpt, then reply to two classmates — especially anyone who predicted a different future than you did.

Accommodations & access. The accessible excerpt + summary let you complete the reading without the scanned PDF; the timeline is keyboard-operable. Respond by typing or recording. Need the excerpt enlarged or in another format? Message your instructor (confidential, per IEP/504).

pages.title: 2.01 A Network of Networks
pages.html:
Unit 2 · Lesson 2.01

A Network of Networks

I can…
  • explain how the Internet joins smaller networks into one world-wide system;
  • trace a message's journey as packets hopping router to router;
  • describe the problem Tim Berners-Lee was trying to solve when he proposed the Web.

🧭 The hook

Send a message to a friend overseas and it arrives in under a second. Nothing physical traveled — yet something crossed oceans, hopped between machines owned by dozens of different organizations, and found one specific device among billions. Nobody runs the whole route. It works because thousands of smaller networks agree to cooperate — a network of networks. That's the Internet.

🛠️ Explore: follow the packets

Step through the Packet Voyage below. Watch how one photo becomes numbered packets, how routers pass them along — sometimes by different roads — and how the pieces reassemble at the destination.

Open in a new tab if needed: Packet Voyage ↗

📜 Primary source: the memo that invented the Web

Tim Berners-Lee, "Information Management: A Proposal." CERN, March 1989. The internal memo that proposed what became the World Wide Web. His boss wrote three words on it: "Vague, but exciting."

📄 Read the proposal (full text, W3C) →

Access: full-text HTML — screen-reader and text-to-speech friendly. Focus on the sections "Losing information at CERN" through "Hypertext." The diagrams are optional.

Context: who, when, why it matters

In 1989, the Internet already existed — computers could exchange data — but information lived in incompatible systems, and finding anything meant knowing exactly where to look. Berners-Lee, a software engineer at CERN (the physics lab in Geneva), watched knowledge evaporate every time someone left the lab. His fix: link documents to each other with hypertext, across any computer, with no central boss. The Web is this memo, grown up.

Read with these questions (for the Agora)

  1. What problem at CERN is Berners-Lee actually trying to solve? (Cite a line — it's not "invent the Web.")
  2. Why does he argue a web of links beats a tree (folders inside folders) for organizing information?
  3. He insisted the system work across different kinds of computers, with no central control. How does that echo how the Internet itself works (think: network of networks)?
  4. Where did his proposal underestimate what the Web would become?

🏛️ Discuss in the Agora

Head to "Vague, but Exciting: the Memo that Made the Web." Post your response to the reading questions (≈150 words, with a cited quote), then reply to two classmates. Lead-learner honesty: some of this memo is dry engineering — dig for the idea underneath, and say what surprised you.

📖 Logbook (quick reflection)

The Internet moves packets; the Web links documents. In your own words — one or two sentences — what's the difference?

pages.title: 2.02 The Parts of a Network
pages.html:
Unit 2 · Lesson 2.02

The Parts of a Network

I can…
  • name the components of a wired network and of a wireless network;
  • explain what it takes for two devices to communicate at all;
  • tell a public IP address from a private one, and say why both exist.

🧭 Two flavors, one recipe

Every network needs the same three ingredients: at least two devices, a way to carry the signal, and addresses so data finds the right machine. The "carry the signal" part comes in two flavors:

Wired networkWireless network
Network interface card (NIC) — the device's wired connection point.Wi-Fi adapter — the device's radio.
Ethernet cable — physically carries the signal.Radio waves — no cable needed.
Network switch — joins several wired devices and forwards traffic between them.Wireless access point — broadcasts the signal devices connect to.

Trade-offs: wires are faster and steadier (great for a desktop or game console that never moves); wireless is flexible and mobile (essential for phones and laptops). Most real networks mix both — your home router usually contains a switch and an access point in one box.

🛠️ Explore: build the parts list

Sort each component into wired, wireless, or both. You can retry until it's perfect — aim for a flawless run.

Open in a new tab if needed: Network Builder ↗

Addresses: how devices are found

Every device on a network has an IP address — its number on the street of the Internet. There are two kinds, and the difference matters:

  • Private addresses (like 192.168.1.12) work only inside your home or school network. Every house can reuse the same private numbers — like apartment numbers that repeat in every building.
  • Public addresses (like 203.0.113.7) are unique across the whole Internet — like a full street address. Your router holds the public address and translates between the two, so one public address can serve every device in the house.

Why both? There aren't enough classic addresses for every gadget on Earth to have its own public one — and keeping devices private adds a layer of protection. (You'll see the security side of this in Unit 7.)

📖 Logbook (quick reflection)

Count the devices on your home network (phones, TVs, consoles, laptops, smart gadgets). Which are wired, which are wireless — and did anything surprise you?

Accommodations & access. The sorter is keyboard-operable with feedback announced to screen readers; the tables restate every fact in text. Respond by typing or recording. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

pages.title: 2.03 When Networks Break
pages.html:
Unit 2 · Lesson 2.03

When Networks Break

I can…
  • name the common issues that slow a network down or take it offline;
  • reason from a symptom ("the Wi-Fi is slow") to a likely cause, like a technician;
  • trace how networking hardware evolved from hubs to fiber optics.

🧭 "The Wi-Fi is down!"

Every household knows the cry. But "the Wi-Fi is down" is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Networks fail for a handful of predictable reasons, and good troubleshooters check them methodically — the same decomposition skill you used in Base Camp.

The usual suspects

IssueWhat it looks likeFirst move
Congestion — too much traffic for the connectionEverything crawls at busy times (four people streaming at once).Pause big downloads/streams; see if speed returns.
Weak signal / interferenceFine near the router, awful two rooms away; microwaves and walls make it worse.Move closer; reduce obstacles; try a wired connection.
Hardware failure — router, cable, NIC, or access pointOne device (or everyone) drops off entirely; a cable looks chewed.Restart gear; swap the cable; check the lights.
Configuration problems — wrong password, bad address settings"Connected, no Internet," or one device can't join while others can.Re-enter credentials; forget & rejoin the network.
Provider outage — the problem is outside your houseEvery device is down; neighbors are down too.Check the provider's status page (on mobile data).

Technician's habit: change one thing at a time, and test after each change — otherwise you never learn which fix worked.

How the gear got here (a two-minute history)

  • Hubs (1980s–90s): the first way to join several computers — but a hub shouts every message to everyone connected. Noisy and slow as networks grew.
  • Switches: the smart successor — a switch learns which device is on which port and delivers each message only to its destination. Hubs are now museum pieces.
  • Ethernet cabling: the wired standard for 50 years, evolving from thick coaxial cable to today's twisted-pair — each generation carrying more data.
  • Wireless (Wi-Fi, late 1990s→): cut the cord; every generation gets faster and handles more devices.
  • Fiber optics: data as pulses of light through glass — the backbone of the modern Internet, crossing oceans on submarine cables.

Notice the same trend you saw in Unit 1: each generation carries more data, more reliably — the network's own Moore's-Law story.

✍️ Do this: play network doctor

Open the assignment "Network Doctor". You'll get two realistic trouble tickets, diagnose the most likely cause for each, and prescribe a first fix — with your reasoning.

pages.title: 2.04 Can You Trust What You Find?
pages.html:
Unit 2 · Lesson 2.04

Can You Trust What You Find?

I can…
  • evaluate an online source for accuracy, relevance, comprehensiveness, and bias;
  • use lateral reading — checking what other sources say about a source;
  • explain why the network that delivers information can't vouch for it.

🧭 The network delivers everything — true or not

Here's the uncomfortable consequence of everything you've learned this unit: the Internet moves packets brilliantly and checks their truth not at all. Berners-Lee built a web where anyone can publish — that's its glory and its hazard. The routers don't care whether a page is a peer-reviewed study or an invented rumor. Quality control is your job. A scholar's tools:

The four tests

TestAsk yourselfRed flag
AccuracyCan I verify these claims in at least one independent, reliable source? Are sources cited?No citations; numbers that appear nowhere else.
RelevanceDoes this actually answer my question — and is it current enough for the topic?A 2009 page answering a question about today's technology.
ComprehensivenessDoes it cover the whole picture, or cherry-pick one side's evidence?No mention of counter-arguments anyone would raise.
BiasWho made this, and what do they gain if I believe it? Is it selling, persuading, or informing?The "study" is hosted by the company whose product it praises.

The professional move: read laterally

Fact-checkers don't stare harder at a suspicious page — they leave it. Open new tabs and search: Who runs this site? What do other sources say about it? Does anyone else report this claim? Two minutes of lateral reading beats twenty minutes of squinting. (Bias isn't automatically disqualifying — every author has a perspective — but you have to know the perspective to weigh the source.)

Open the assignment "Source Detective". You'll pick one online source you'd actually use for the unit project, run it through all four tests plus a lateral read, and render a verdict: use it, use it with caution, or reject it — with evidence.

pages.title: 3.01 The First Programmer
pages.html:
Unit 3 · Lesson 3.01

The First Programmer

I can…
  • explain why Ada Lovelace is called the first programmer — a century before computers existed;
  • classify programming languages by paradigm and by what they're used for;
  • write and run my first program in a browser-based editor.

🧭 The hook

In 1843 — no electricity in homes, no computers, Darwin hadn't published — a 27-year-old mathematician wrote instructions for a machine that existed only on paper, and in doing so saw further than anyone alive: that a machine for numbers could one day manipulate symbols, music, anything. Her name was Ada Lovelace, and her "Note G" is often called the first computer program.

📜 Primary source: Lovelace's Notes (1843)

Ada Lovelace, translator's Notes on L. F. Menabrea's Sketch of the Analytical Engine (1843) — especially Note A and Note G. Her notes ran three times longer than the paper she was translating.

📄 Read the full text (HTML) →

Access: full accessible HTML. It's long and Victorian — read the two key passages quoted below plus a skim of Note G's opening; the guided questions only need those.

The two passages that matter most

"We may say most aptly, that the Analytical Engine weaves algebraical patterns just as the Jacquard-loom weaves flowers and leaves." (Note A)

"The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything. It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform. It can follow analysis; but it has no power of anticipating any analytical relations or truths." (Note G)

In plain language: (1) a machine that manipulates symbols by rules can "weave" anything expressible in symbols — that's software; and (2) the machine only does what it's told — every program is our thinking, made executable. A century later, Alan Turing named this second claim "Lady Lovelace's objection" and argued with it — you'll meet that debate again in Unit 8.

Read with these questions (for the Agora)

  1. What does the weaving metaphor claim a computing machine can do beyond arithmetic? (Quote the line.)
  2. Lovelace says the Engine "has no pretensions whatever to originate anything." Do you agree — can a machine only ever do what we order it to? What about today's AI?
  3. Why might it matter that this insight came from someone trained in both mathematics and the arts?

From Note G to now: the languages

Lovelace wrote her "program" as a table of operations. Today we write in programming languages, and they sort into families:

How they organize thinking (paradigm)What that means
ProceduralA recipe: step-by-step instructions and reusable procedures. (C, and the style you'll start in.)
Object-orientedA cast of characters: bundles of data + behavior ("objects") that interact. (Java, Python, JavaScript can all work this way.)

Languages also specialize by domain: some are built for scientific work (heavy math, data, simulations — Python, R, MATLAB), others thrive in commercial applications (websites, apps, business systems — JavaScript, Java, C#). Same big ideas everywhere; the accent changes.

🛠️ Explore: your first program in a real IDE

Programmers work in an IDE (integrated development environment) — an editor that also runs, tests, and helps debug your code. You'll use two free, browser-based ones all unit:

  • Code.org App Lab ↗ — build apps with blocks or JavaScript text (you can toggle between them).
  • p5.js Web Editor ↗ — creative coding: draw and animate with JavaScript.

Open the assignment "First Sketch" and follow its steps: you'll make a p5.js sketch run, change it, break it on purpose, and fix it — your first full write→run→test→debug loop.

🏛️ Discuss in the Agora

Head to "The Enchantress of Numbers: Can Machines Originate?" Post your take on Lovelace's claim (with a quoted line), then reply to two classmates.

Accommodations & access. The required passages are quoted on this page with a plain-language summary; the full text is accessible HTML. Both IDEs run in the browser; App Lab's block mode is a supported starting point. Respond by typing or recording. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

pages.title: 3.02 Functions, Input & Output
pages.html:
Unit 3 · Lesson 3.02

Functions, Input & Output

I can…
  • write a function — a named, reusable code segment — and pass it arguments;
  • write a program that takes input from a user and produces output;
  • write prompts so clear that a stranger knows exactly what to type.

🧭 Name it once, use it forever

You already met the input→process→output loop in Unit 1 as hardware. Now you'll build it in software. And the single most important tool for organizing software is the function: a chunk of code with a name, so you can use it a thousand times without writing it twice.

Anatomy of a function

function greet(name) {            // "greet" is the NAME; "name" is a PARAMETER
  return "Welcome, " + name + "!"; // what the function gives back
}

greet("Ada");     // → "Welcome, Ada!"   ← "Ada" is the ARGUMENT you pass in
greet("Grace");   // → "Welcome, Grace!" ← same code, different input
  • Define once — the function is a recipe with a name.
  • Call anywhere — each call can pass different arguments, so one function handles endless cases.
  • Different languages call them functions, subroutines, or methods — same idea: a reusable code segment.

Programs that listen: input → process → output

A program without input always does the same thing. Add input and it becomes a conversation:

var name = promptStr("What's your first name?");   // INPUT (App Lab)
var message = greet(name);                          // PROCESS (your function!)
write(message);                                     // OUTPUT

In p5.js, input can also be the mouse and keyboard — mouseX, mouseIsPressed, keyPressed() — and output is what you draw. Input doesn't have to be typed text.

The craft of the prompt

The user can't read your mind — only your prompt. Compare:

😕 Vague prompt✅ Clear prompt
"Enter date""Enter your birth date as MM/DD/YYYY (e.g., 03/14/2011)"
"Number?""How many tickets? Enter a whole number from 1 to 10"

A clear prompt states what to enter, in what format, with an example or range. (In 3.05 you'll add the second half of this craft: validating what actually comes back.)

🛠️ Practice (in your IDE)

In App Lab or p5.js, build a mini "greeter": ask for a name (clear prompt!), pass it through a function that builds a message, and output the result. Then call the same function three times with different arguments — feel the reuse. Keep this sketch: it becomes a seed for the unit project.

📖 Logbook (quick reflection)

Where in your daily life do you follow a "function" — a named routine you run with slightly different inputs each time? (Getting-ready-for-school with different wake-up times counts.)

Accommodations & access. All code samples are provided as selectable text (screen-reader friendly). Block mode in App Lab is a supported path. Respond by typing or recording. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

pages.title: 3.03 Making Decisions, Going in Circles
pages.html:
Unit 3 · Lesson 3.03

Making Decisions, Going in Circles

I can…
  • use selection (if / else if / else) so my program chooses between paths;
  • use iteration (loops) — including a loop inside a loop — to repeat work;
  • decide when code should run once, conditionally, or repeatedly.

🧭 Two superpowers

So far your programs run straight through, top to bottom — a non-iterative sequence. Two structures turn that straight line into real behavior: selection (choose a path) and iteration (repeat a path). Master these two and you can express almost any procedure.

Selection: the fork in the road

if (temperature > 90) {
  write("Stay hydrated out there!");
} else if (temperature > 60) {
  write("Beautiful day.");
} else {
  write("Bring a jacket.");
}
  • The condition in parentheses is a Boolean question — true or false (more on those in 3.04).
  • Exactly one branch runs. The chain is checked top to bottom; the first true condition wins.
  • else is the catch-all — it runs when nothing above was true.

Iteration: the loop

for (var i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {   // start at 1; keep going while i ≤ 5; add 1 each time
  write("Lap " + i);
}
// Lap 1  Lap 2  Lap 3  Lap 4  Lap 5

A while loop repeats as long as a condition stays true — perfect when you don't know the count in advance ("keep asking until the answer is valid" — you'll use exactly that in 3.05).

Loops inside loops (nesting)

for (var row = 1; row <= 3; row++) {      // outer loop: each row
  for (var seat = 1; seat <= 4; seat++) {  // inner loop: each seat IN that row
    write("Row " + row + ", Seat " + seat);
  }
}   // 3 rows × 4 seats = 12 lines — the inner loop runs fully for every outer pass

Nested loops are how programs handle grids: pixels on a screen, seats in a theater, cells in a spreadsheet. In p5.js, two nested loops can paint an entire checkerboard in four lines.

Which structure when?

You want to…Reach for
Do steps once, in orderPlain sequence (non-iterative)
Do something only in certain casesSelection — if / else if / else
Repeat a known number of timesfor loop
Repeat until a condition changeswhile loop
Work through a gridNested loops

🛠️ Practice (in your IDE)

Two quick builds — do at least one, keep both if you can:

  1. Decision machine (App Lab): extend your greeter — ask for an age and reply differently for at least three age ranges (if / else if / else).
  2. Pattern weaver (p5.js): use nested loops to draw a grid of shapes; make the color depend on an if so a checkerboard appears. (Lovelace would approve — you're literally weaving patterns.)
Accommodations & access. Code samples are selectable text; the decision table restates the concepts. Block mode remains a supported path. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

Next: 3.04 — The Logic Inside →

pages.title: 3.04 The Logic Inside
pages.html:
Unit 3 · Lesson 3.04

The Logic Inside

I can…
  • evaluate Boolean expressions using AND, OR, and NOT;
  • use standard logic operators inside a program's conditions;
  • predict the value of an arithmetic expression using operator precedence.

🧭 Two values, three operators, all of computing

Underneath every if-statement, every search filter, every game rule sits Boolean logic — named for George Boole, who showed in the 1850s that reasoning itself could be done as algebra on just two values: true and false. Three operators combine them, and combinations of those three build everything.

🛠️ Explore: the Boolean Logic Lab

Flip the switches, watch six expressions update live, then take the predict-the-output challenge. Aim for 5/5.

Open in a new tab if needed: Boolean Logic Lab ↗

In real code

In JavaScript (App Lab and p5.js), the operators are written && (AND), || (OR), ! (NOT), alongside comparisons like >= and ==:

if (age >= 13 && age <= 19) {         // AND: both must be true → a teenager
  write("Teen ticket");
}
if (day == "Sat" || day == "Sun") {   // OR: either one → the weekend
  write("Sleep in!");
}
if (!loggedIn) {                       // NOT: flip it → not logged in
  write("Please sign in first.");
}

🛠️ Explore: the order of operations

Booleans decide which path runs; arithmetic decides what values flow through it — and computers evaluate arithmetic in a strict order. Step through each expression and predict before you click:

Open in a new tab if needed: Order of Operations Stepper ↗

The traps to remember: multiplication/division outrank addition/subtraction; ties go left to right; and parentheses beat everything — when in doubt, add parentheses and make your intention unmissable.

🛠️ Practice (in your IDE)

Upgrade your 3.03 decision machine with compound conditions: a ticket-price program where age AND day of week together pick the price (e.g., kids on weekends ride free). You'll need &&, ||, and at least one calculation whose precedence you had to think about.

pages.title: 3.05 When Code Breaks
pages.html:
Unit 3 · Lesson 3.05

When Code Breaks

I can…
  • identify the four kinds of programming errors from their symptoms;
  • debug methodically: reproduce, isolate, fix, re-test;
  • validate user input so bad data can't crash or corrupt my program.

🧭 Errors are the curriculum

Here's a professional secret: everyone's code breaks, constantly. The difference between a beginner and an expert isn't fewer errors — it's how fast they read an error and know where to look. On this expedition, a bug isn't a failure; it's a discovery with a sticker on it telling you what to learn next.

🛠️ Explore: Bug Triage

Eight real-world bug tickets. Classify each as a syntax, runtime, logic, or computation error — the four kinds you'll meet forever.

Open in a new tab if needed: Bug Triage ↗

Debugging like a scientist

  1. Reproduce it. Make the bug happen on demand — a bug you can't reproduce is a rumor.
  2. Read the message. Error messages name the line and the complaint. Start there, not at line 1.
  3. Isolate it. Comment out chunks, or print values mid-run, until you corner the failing piece (decomposition again!).
  4. Fix one thing, then re-test. Change two things at once and you won't know which mattered — the same rule your Network Doctor training used.

Defensive programming: validate the input

In 3.02 you wrote clear prompts. But users still type the unexpected — "twelve" instead of 12, a birthday in the wrong format, nothing at all. A professional program checks input before using it:

var tickets = promptNum("How many tickets? (1-10)");
while (tickets < 1 || tickets > 10) {                 // a while loop stands guard
  tickets = promptNum("Please enter a number from 1 to 10:");
}
write("You reserved " + tickets + " tickets.");        // only valid data gets through

Notice the teamwork: a while loop (3.03) + a Boolean condition (3.04) + a clear re-prompt (3.02) = input validation. Everything in this unit clicks together here — and it prevents the runtime and computation errors you just triaged.

pages.title: 4.01 The Anatomy of an Algorithm
pages.html:
Unit 4 · Lesson 4.01

The Anatomy of an Algorithm

I can…
  • name the four building blocks of algorithms — sequence, selection, iteration, recursion;
  • decompose a problem into new, smaller pieces of code;
  • explain why Dijkstra argued that program structure is what lets humans trust code.

🧭 Four blocks build everything

Every algorithm ever written — from a recipe to a rocket controller — is assembled from just four moves. Three you already used in Unit 3. The fourth is new, and it's a mind-bender:

BlockThe moveYou've seen it as…
SequenceDo steps in order.Every program, top to bottom.
SelectionChoose a path.if / else if / else (3.03).
IterationRepeat a path.for / while loops (3.03).
RecursionA procedure that calls itself on a smaller piece of the problem, until the piece is small enough to answer directly.New! See below.

Recursion in one story

You're at the back of a long line and want to know your position. You can't see the front — so you ask the person ahead: "What's your position?" They don't know either, so they ask the person ahead of them… until the question reaches the front. "I'm first!" Then the answers roll back: second, third, fourth… down to you. One tiny procedure — ask ahead, add one — solved the whole line by calling itself on a smaller line. The "I'm first" moment is the base case: the point where recursion stops. Every correct recursion has one, or it asks forever.

📜 Primary source: Dijkstra's furious little letter (1968)

Edsger W. Dijkstra, "Go To Statement Considered Harmful." Communications of the ACM, Vol. 11, No. 3 (March 1968). Two pages that started a decades-long argument about how code should be built.

📄 Read the letter (PDF) →

Access note: the PDF is a scan, so screen readers can't read it aloud. The key passages are quoted below with a plain-language summary — that's the required reading path.

Accessible excerpt (the heart of the argument)

"For a number of years I have been familiar with the observation that the quality of programmers is a decreasing function of the density of go to statements in the programs they produce."

"…our intellectual powers are rather geared to master static relations and… our powers to visualize processes evolving in time are relatively poorly developed. For that reason we should… shorten the conceptual gap between the static program and the dynamic process."

In plain language: 1968 programs were full of go to — an instruction that jumps anywhere in the code, from anywhere. The result was "spaghetti": programs no human could follow. Dijkstra's claim is really about human minds: we're good at reading things that stand still (a page of structured code) and terrible at imagining tangled processes jumping through time. So build programs only from structures a mind can follow — sequence, selection, iteration (and disciplined recursion). Your generation learned it that way from day one because he won this argument.

Read with these questions (for the Agora)

  1. What exactly does Dijkstra say human minds are good and bad at? (Quote the excerpt.)
  2. His title says a tool is "harmful" — not broken, not slow, but harmful to the people using it. Is code clarity a technical preference or something closer to an ethical duty when others must trust your program?
  3. Where else (outside programming) do we ban a "works fine" shortcut because it makes things impossible to check?

🏛️ Discuss in the Agora

Head to "Considered Harmful: Is Clear Code a Moral Duty?" Post (with a quoted line), then reply to two classmates.

📖 Logbook (quick reflection)

pages.title: 4.02 Judging Algorithms
pages.html:
Unit 4 · Lesson 4.02

Judging Algorithms

I can…
  • compare two algorithms with evidence (counting steps, testing multiple inputs);
  • judge an algorithm by all three tests: efficiency, correctness, and clarity;
  • explain why the "faster" algorithm sometimes isn't the right choice.

🧭 Same problem, different costs

Two algorithms can both be correct and yet be worlds apart in cost. Searching a sorted list is the classic showcase: checking every item works — but exploiting the sorting works exponentially better. Don't take my word for it. Run the race.

🛠️ Explore: the Algorithm Race

Race linear search against binary search. Try at least three targets: one near the start, one near the end, one in the middle. Watch the comparison counters — they're your evidence.

Open in a new tab if needed: Algorithm Race ↗

Why binary search wins: halving

Every binary-search comparison throws away half of what's left. 15 items → at most 4 checks. A million items → at most 20. A billion → about 30. Linear search's cost grows with the list; binary search's cost grows with the number of times you can halve the list — barely at all. That's what "more efficient" means, measured, not vibed.

But notice the fine print: binary search only works because the list was sorted. On an unsorted list it's simply wrong — fast nonsense. Which brings us to the full scorecard:

The three tests

TestThe questionHow you check
CorrectnessDoes it give the right answer — for every valid input?Test many inputs, especially edge cases (first item, last item, missing item).
EfficiencyHow does the cost grow as the input grows?Count steps/comparisons; compare execution on small vs. large inputs.
ClarityCan another human read, trust, and fix it?The Dijkstra test: structured, well-named, no spaghetti.

Real engineers weigh all three. A slightly slower algorithm that's obviously correct and readable often beats a clever one nobody can maintain — unless the input is huge and efficiency is everything. Judgment, with evidence.

Open the assignment "Algorithm Autopsy" — you'll gather comparison-count evidence from the race, design your own everyday algorithm two different ways, and rule which version wins each of the three tests.

pages.title: 4.03 The Data Expedition
pages.html:
Unit 4 · Lesson 4.03

The Data Expedition

I can…
  • run advanced searches that find what a plain search can't;
  • design a plan for collecting original data — and defend its fairness;
  • separate usable data from noise, and describe how massive datasets get analyzed.

🧭 Algorithms are engines; data is fuel

Your rumor simulation next lesson, every chart in the news, every AI you've ever used — all of them are only as good as the data underneath. Getting good data is a skill with three parts: finding it, collecting it, and filtering it.

Finding: search like a professional

You evaluated sources in Unit 2. Now upgrade the searching itself — a few operators turn a vague query into a scalpel:

OperatorWhat it doesExample
"exact phrase"Match these words, in this order"screen time" teens sleep
site:Only results from one site/domainsite:.gov air quality florida
-wordExclude a wordjaguar speed -car
filetype:Only a specific file kindhurricane data filetype:csv
Date filterOnly recent results (search Tools menu)past year only

Collecting: design before you gather

When the data you need doesn't exist yet, you collect it — and the design of the collection decides whether the data means anything:

  • Question first. "Do students who sleep more feel more alert?" — the question dictates what to measure.
  • Define the measurement. Exactly what will you record, in what units, how often? ("Hours of sleep, to the half hour, self-reported each morning for a week.")
  • Mind the sample. Who's included? Ten friends from one class isn't "students in general." A survey only night-owls answer is already biased.
  • Keep it ethical. Get consent, anonymize, collect only what the question needs — data about people is a responsibility (much more in Units 7–8).

Filtering: usable data vs. noise

Raw data arrives messy. Before analysis, a scientist asks of every column and row: does this help answer my question?

Mini-exercise (think, then reveal in the Logbook): your sleep survey came back with these fields — bedtime, hours slept, alertness rating, favorite pizza topping, the respondent's name spelled three ways, one entry claiming "25 hours." Which are usable data, which are miscellaneous information, and which are errors to clean? What would you do with the "25 hours" row — and does deleting it feel different from correcting it?

When data gets massive

Your survey fits in a spreadsheet. But a hospital network, a streaming service, or a weather agency generates more data per hour than one computer can hold. Analyzing at that scale uses different techniques:

  • Sampling — analyze a well-chosen slice instead of everything (like tasting the soup, not drinking the pot).
  • Divide & combine — split the data across hundreds of machines, let each analyze its piece, then merge the results (decomposition at warehouse scale).
  • Streaming — analyze data as it flows past, keeping running totals instead of storing every record.
  • Visualization — turn millions of rows into a picture a human can actually judge.

Different tools, same principle you've used since Base Camp: decompose the problem until each piece is manageable.

pages.title: 4.04 Models, Simulations & Learning Machines
pages.html:
Unit 4 · Lesson 4.04

Models, Simulations & Learning Machines

I can…
  • use a simulation to find patterns and test a hypothesis against data;
  • explain what a model leaves out — and why that's the point;
  • train a simple machine-learning model and describe how predictive AI forecasts the future.

🧭 A model is a useful lie

A subway map lies about distances — usefully (that was abstraction, Base Camp). A model does the same to a whole system: keep the forces that matter, drop the rest, and you get a miniature world you can experiment on. Make the model run over time and you have a simulation — a laboratory for questions too big, slow, dangerous, or expensive to test in reality. Will the hurricane hit Tampa? Nobody runs the hurricane twice. They run the model ten thousand times.

🛠️ Explore: the Rumor Mill

Do real science in miniature: set parameters → state a hypothesis → run 30 trials → face the data. Then change one parameter at a time and find out which lever actually matters.

Open in a new tab if needed: Simulation Sandbox ↗

Three habits of honest modelers — use them in your capstone:

  • Run it many times. One run of a random process proves nothing; the pattern across runs is the finding.
  • Change one parameter at a time — or you won't know what caused the difference (your debugging rule, again).
  • Ask what the model ignores. The Rumor Mill assumes everyone talks to everyone. Real schools have friend groups. Does that make its prediction too fast or too slow? Knowing a model's limits is part of the result.

🛠️ Explore: teach a machine

So far you wrote every rule. Machine learning flips it: show the computer labeled examples, and it finds the pattern itself. Try it — no code required:

Google Teachable Machine ↗ (free, browser-based, no account needed)

  1. New Image Project (or Audio/Pose if you prefer — all count).
  2. Make two classes — e.g., "thumbs up" vs. "thumbs down," or two objects from your desk. Record ~30 samples of each.
  3. Train, then test live. Now try to fool it: weird angles, bad lighting, an object it never saw.

Notice what you just did: your samples were the data, training found the pattern, and the fooling was a hypothesis test — the same loop as the Rumor Mill, but the machine built the model. And notice what decided its quality: your data. Thirty photos from one angle make a brittle model — exactly why the data-collection design you learned in 4.03 matters.

Predictive AI: models that forecast

Feed the learning loop historical data and it can forecast: tomorrow's weather from decades of atmospheres, a stock's movement from market history, a team's win chance from seasons of stats, your next show from your watch history. Predictive AI is pattern-finding pointed at the future — and it inherits every limit you've met today: it's only as good as its data, and it fails where the future stops resembling the past. (Where these systems shine and where they break — medicine, cars, space — is a Unit 8 story; you now own the concepts underneath it.)

📖 Logbook (quick reflection)

Your Teachable Machine model: what fooled it, and what about your training data explains why?

  1. Make it run. Open the p5.js Web Editor (free; create an account so you can save). Start a new sketch, paste in the starter code from lesson 3.01's assignment page, and press ▶. Move your mouse over the canvas — that's input → process → output, live.
    function setup() { createCanvas(400, 400); }
    function draw() { background(14, 28, 66); fill(85, 200, 232); circle(mouseX, mouseY, 50); }
  2. Make it yours. Change at least three things — colors, shape, size, background — and describe what each change did.
  3. Break it on purpose. Delete one parenthesis or bracket. Run it. Read the error message. In 1–2 sentences: what did the editor tell you, and what kind of error was it? Fix it.
  4. Classify your tools. In 2–3 sentences: the editor you used is an IDE — what did it do for you besides hold text? And was the language used here for a scientific or a creative/commercial kind of task?
  5. Submit your sketch's share link (File → Share) + your answers.

Prefer blocks? Code.org App Lab is an equal alternative — do the same steps and submit an App Lab share link.

Accommodations: no time limit; block-based path fully accepted; respond by typing or recording. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

assignments.title: Bug Hunt
assignments.html:
Submit the fixed program's share link plus your bug report (typed or recorded).

A "colleague" left you a broken ticket-price program. Fix it, document it, and bulletproof it.

  1. Recreate the broken program in App Lab (or p5.js with prompts) — bugs included:
    var age = promptNum("Enter");
    if (age > 12) { write("Child ticket: $5") } else { write("Adult ticket: $10"); }
    var total = age + 2 * 10;
    write("Family total: $" + total);
  2. Hunt the bugs. There are at least three: one that stops the program or complains immediately; one that makes the wrong branch run (kids are being charged as adults!); and one calculation that doesn't match its intent ("age plus 2, times 10"). Also: that prompt is terrible.
  3. File your bug report. For each bug: quote the line, name the error type (syntax / logic / runtime / computation), explain the fix.
  4. Bulletproof it. Rewrite the prompt so it's clear, and add input validation (a while loop) so an age below 0 or above 120 gets re-asked instead of accepted.
  5. Submit the working program's share link + your report.

Accommodations: no time limit; block mode accepted; report by typing or recording. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

assignments.title: The Interactive Machine (Unit 3 Project)
assignments.html:
Submit a share link + a short written or recorded walkthrough.

Design and build a small interactive program — your choice of idea, meeting this spec. Ideas: a quiz game, a ticket-price calculator, an adventure with choices, a pattern generator the user controls, a study-timer, a pet simulator.

The spec — your program must include all of these:

  1. Input & output: it takes input from the user (typed, clicked, or keyboard/mouse) and produces output that depends on it.
  2. At least one function you wrote, called more than once or with different arguments.
  3. Selection: an if / else if / else with at least two genuinely different paths.
  4. Iteration: at least one loop doing real work (repetition, retry, or drawing).
  5. A compound condition using && or ||.
  6. Clear prompts + input validation: invalid input gets re-asked, not a crash.
  7. Tested: you ran it with at least three different inputs, including one designed to break it.

The walkthrough: name where each spec item lives in your code, and describe one bug you hit while building and how you fixed it. (You must be able to explain every line — AI help is fine with disclosure, per our class agreement.)

Platform: Code.org App Lab or p5.js — blocks or text both count. Scope guide: 30–80 lines is plenty.

Accommodations: no time limit; blocks or text; walkthrough by typing or recording. Extended options per IEP/504 (confidential).

assignments.title: VR Build — Walk the Logic
assignments.html:
VR Build · Arthur · Build it yourself
Walk the Logic 🚶
There's no room or experience waiting for you — you build the flowchart yourself in an empty Arthur space.
How to turn it in — your choice. Either (A) a few in-headset screenshots + a short written reflection, or (B) a short recorded video walkthrough. Both earn equal credit.

A flowchart on paper is something you read. Build one you can walk. Invent any simple program (a ticket-price check, a "what to wear" decider, a login gate) and construct it life-size in your own Arthur space:

  1. Start / input node — where a value enters the program.
  2. A function box — a labeled step you could reuse (e.g., "check age", "roll again"). Show it used at least twice, or with different inputs.
  3. A decision fork — an if / else with two genuinely different paths a walker can take.
  4. A loop — a path that visibly circles back to repeat a step, with a clear way out.
  5. An output — where the result comes out.

Then walk one sample input through the whole chart and, in your submission, narrate the exact route the "data" takes and why it went that way at the fork.

Accommodations & comfort. Self-paced, no time limit. Use Arthur's comfort settings (teleport, vignette, seated mode) and stop if you feel unwell. Type or dictate labels; submit screenshots or video. If your IEP/504 or device access calls for an equivalent non-VR build (Tinkercad/CoSpaces or a slide-based spatial walkthrough), you'll receive full credit — arrange confidentially with your instructor.

assignments.title: Algorithm Autopsy
assignments.html:
Submit as text, or a recorded walkthrough.

Judge algorithms like an engineer — with evidence.

Part 1 — Gather race evidence. In the Algorithm Race (lesson 4.02), run at least three races with different targets (one near the start, one near the end, one in the middle). Record a small table: target · linear comparisons · binary comparisons. Then answer: when does linear search come closest to winning, and why does binary search dominate everywhere else?

Part 2 — Design one algorithm, two ways. Pick an everyday task (finding a name in a contact list, choosing what to wear by weather, locating a book on a shelf). Write two different algorithms for it as numbered steps — a straightforward version and a cleverer version (sorting first, splitting in half, checking common cases first…).

Part 3 — Render the verdict. Score your two versions on the three tests — correctness (any inputs where it fails?), efficiency (which takes fewer steps as the task grows?), clarity (which would a stranger follow more easily?). Declare a winner for a stated situation — and name a situation where the other one would win.

Accommodations: no time limit; steps may be written, dictated, or drawn as a flowchart. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

assignments.title: The Data Expedition Plan
assignments.html:
Submit as text + screenshots, or a recorded walkthrough.

Every expedition needs supplies. Yours needs data — found and gathered.

Part 1 — Advanced-search safari. Pick any research question you care about. Run it as a plain search, then improve it twice using operators from lesson 4.03 ("exact phrase", site:, -exclude, filetype:, date filter). Submit: your three queries (plain → better → best), a screenshot of the best results, and 2–3 sentences on what each refinement changed.

Part 2 — Design an original-data collection. For the same question (or a new one), write a plan you could genuinely run this month: Question (one sentence) · Measurement (exactly what you'll record, units, how often) · Sample (who/what, how many, and one bias your sample might have — be honest) · Ethics line (consent / anonymity / only-what's-needed).

Part 3 — Pre-filter the mess. List 4–6 fields your collection could produce. Mark each usable data or miscellaneous, and describe one bad entry you'd expect (a "25-hour day") and what you'd do with it.

Part 4 — Scale thought (2–3 sentences). If your collection suddenly had a million entries, which massive-data technique (sampling, divide & combine, streaming, visualization) would you reach for first, and why?

Tip: do this well and it becomes the data plan for your Semester 1 capstone.

Accommodations: no time limit; screenshots optional if queries are described precisely; respond by typing or recording. Alternative formats on request (confidential, per IEP/504).

assignments.title: Model the World (Semester 1 Capstone)
assignments.html:
Submit artifact link(s) + a short presentation or recorded walkthrough.

Close Semester 1 by doing what computational thinkers do: pick a question about the real world, build a miniature of it, and test what you believe against what the model says.

  1. Choose a question you can model. Examples (yours is welcome): how fast a rumor/trend spreads if each person reaches N others (adapt the Rumor Mill); whether a checkout line moves faster with one shared line or one per register; how many games a tournament needs so the better team usually wins; whether a machine can learn to tell your two sketches/objects/sounds apart — and what breaks it (Teachable Machine route).
  2. State your hypothesis first. One sentence, written before you run anything: "I predict ___ because ___."
  3. Design the algorithm behind your model. As numbered steps or code: what does one "round" of your simulation do? Inputs, the repeated step, what you record. (p5.js/App Lab if you code it; the Simulation Sandbox, a spreadsheet, or dice-and-paper runs are all legitimate models.)
  4. Run it and gather data. Many trials, not one (30 is a good target if runs are quick). Record results in a table.
  5. Face the data. Show your results two ways (table + chart, or chart + written summary). State the verdict honestly — a busted hypothesis with a good explanation scores better than a lucky guess.
  6. Name the model's limits. Two things your model ignores about reality, and whether each makes its answer too optimistic or too pessimistic.
  7. Present it. Slides or a recorded walkthrough: question → hypothesis → model design → data → verdict → limits. This is your Semester 1 showcase.

Accommodations: no time limit; model medium is your choice (code not required); presentation as slides, recording, or illustrated report. Extended options per IEP/504 (confidential).

assignments.title: VR Build — The Algorithm Arena
assignments.html:
VR Build · Arthur · Build it yourself
The Algorithm Arena 🏁
There's no room or experience waiting for you — you build the arena yourself in an empty Arthur space.
How to turn it in — your choice. Either (A) a few in-headset screenshots + a short written reflection, or (B) a short recorded video walkthrough. Both earn equal credit.

You judged algorithms with a stopwatch. Now make the contest physical. Pick one option and build it from scratch:

Option A — Search race. Build a row of numbered boxes (10–16, in order). Stage a walkable race between linear search and binary search for one target: mark, in order, which boxes each strategy checks. Make the difference visible — linear plods box by box; binary leaps to the middle and halves the field. State the count for each.

Option B — 3D data visualization. Take a small dataset (≤12 honest values). Build it as a 3D bar/pillar chart you can walk among, with labeled axes and a title.

Then, whichever you built, deliver the verdict: which approach or representation is better, for what situation — and name one situation where the other one wins.

Accommodations & comfort. Self-paced, no time limit. Use Arthur's comfort settings (teleport, vignette, seated mode) and stop if you feel unwell. Type or dictate labels; submit screenshots or video. If your IEP/504 or device access calls for an equivalent non-VR build (Tinkercad/CoSpaces or a slide-based spatial walkthrough), you'll receive full credit — arrange confidentially with your instructor.
