discussions.title: Agora — Introductions & Is CS a Liberal Art?
discussions.html:
Welcome to the Agora — our place to think together. This course is asynchronous, so your posts are your presence here.

Part 1 — Introduce yourself (2 sentences). What brought you to this course, and one thing about computing you're curious about?

Part 2 — Respond to Wing (~150–200 words). Do you find Jeannette Wing's argument that computational thinking is "a fundamental skill for everyone" convincing? Quote one line from the essay as evidence (with a reference), and give one example from your own life where computational thinking would help. Optionally, name one place you'd push back.

Part 3 — Reply to two classmates. Build on an idea, ask a genuine question, or respectfully disagree with a reason. "I agree!" is not a reply.

Norms: cite your evidence, use a respectful scholarly voice, and respond — don't just post. You may type or record audio/video for any part.

discussions.title: Moore's Law: Trend or Destiny?
discussions.html:
Gordon Moore predicted a trend in 1965 — and it held for about 50 years. But a trend is not a law of nature.

Post (~150 words): Do you think the pace of hardware improvement Moore described will keep going, slow down, or stop? Quote one line from Moore's excerpt (lesson 1.04) as evidence, and give one example from your own life of a prediction of his that came true. Then make your own forecast: what is the next milestone on the timeline?

Reply to two classmates — especially anyone who forecast a different future than you did. Build on their reasoning or offer a respectful counter-argument with a reason.

Norms: cite your evidence, use a respectful scholarly voice, and respond — don't just post. You may type or record.

discussions.title: Vague, but Exciting: the Memo that Made the Web
discussions.html:
In 1989, Tim Berners-Lee's boss read this memo and wrote three words on the cover: "Vague, but exciting." It became the World Wide Web.

Post (~150 words): What problem was Berners-Lee actually trying to solve at CERN? Quote one line from the proposal (lesson 2.01) as evidence. Then: he argued a web of links would beat a tree of folders for organizing information — do you buy it? Point to one thing in your daily life that works the way he predicted, and one place where his proposal underestimated what the Web would become.

Reply to two classmates. Build on their reading, ask a genuine question, or respectfully push back with a reason.

Norms: cite your evidence, use a respectful scholarly voice, and respond — don't just post. You may type or record.

discussions.title: The Enchantress of Numbers: Can Machines Originate?
discussions.html:
In 1843, Ada Lovelace made two claims about computing machines — a century before one was built:

  1. A machine that follows rules can "weave algebraical patterns" — it could work with any symbols, not just numbers (music, words, pictures).
  2. "The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything. It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform."

Post (~150 words): Was she right on both counts? Quote one of her lines (lesson 3.01) as evidence. Claim 1 clearly came true — your phone weaves music, video, and games from rules. But claim 2 is now hotly debated: when a modern AI writes a poem or code, is it "originating," or still only doing what we ordered it to do, at a very long distance? Take a side and defend it.

Reply to two classmates — especially someone on the other side. Build on or respectfully challenge their reasoning.

Norms: cite your evidence, use a respectful scholarly voice, and respond — don't just post. You may type or record.

discussions.title: Considered Harmful: Is Clear Code a Moral Duty?
discussions.html:
In 1968, Dijkstra didn't call the go to statement slow or buggy — he called it harmful, because it produced programs human minds couldn't follow or trust. He won: the structures you use today (sequence, selection, iteration) are the result.

Post (~150 words): Is writing clear, followable code just a style preference — or something closer to an ethical duty when other people must trust and maintain your program? Quote one line from the excerpt (lesson 4.01) as evidence. Then give one example from outside programming where we ban a "works fine" shortcut because it makes things impossible for others to check (showing your work in math, food labeling, financial records…).

Reply to two classmates. Build on their example, test their reasoning, or respectfully disagree with a reason.

Norms: cite your evidence, use a respectful scholarly voice, and respond — don't just post. You may type or record.
